652.title: Indrajit's death
652.hook: Indrajit kills Sita in front of Hanuman, or seems to
652.howItsDone: Some Ramayana tellers use the illusory Sita, the māyā-sītā of this episode, to talk about māyā, illusion, and how fear can make what is false look real.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Hanuman Chalisa, and how two herb flights became one picture on shrine walls. The one who brings healing.

Indrajit rides out of Lanka's western gate with a woman in his chariot. She's thin, in a soiled garment, weeping, calling Rama's name. Hanuman sees her and freezes. He sat in the tree above her in the ashoka grove; he knows that face. It's Sita. In front of the whole monkey army, Indrajit seizes her by the hair, draws his sword, and cuts her down. Then he shouts across the field: there's nothing left to fight for now.
screen: `A WOMAN IN THE CHARIOT.` → `HANUMAN FREEZES.` → `NOTHING LEFT TO FIGHT FOR.`

segments.voice: Hanuman, who crossed the sea to find her, pulls the army back in despair and goes to tell Rama. Rama, hearing it, collapses. Lakshmana holds him and, in grief, rails against a world where doing right seems to bring only suffering. Then Vibhishana arrives, the one person in the camp who knows how Lanka thinks. That wasn't Sita, he says. Ravana would never allow her to be killed; he wants her too much. It was an illusion, a magic double, and a distraction. Right now Indrajit is on his way to Nikumbhila, a sacred grove and shrine, to complete a fire offering. If he finishes it, he'll be unbeatable. But Brahma's boon has a condition: whoever attacks him there, before the rite is done, can kill him. So send Lakshmana now. Look at what Indrajit has done. He didn't need to win a battle. He needed a few hours, and he knew exactly what would stop his enemies cold: the sight of the person they love most, dying. It's a cruel weapon, because it doesn't touch the body. It goes straight for the heart, and for a while it works. What breaks the spell isn't strength. It's a calm voice that knows the enemy, saying: look again; this isn't what it seems. Rama, steadied, sends Lakshmana off with Vibhishana, Hanuman and an army. The race to Nikumbhila begins.
screen: `RAMA COLLAPSES.` · `VIBHISHANA: IT WAS AN ILLUSION.` · `THE FIRE AT NIKUMBHILA.` · `A WEAPON AIMED AT THE HEART.` · then, large: `LOOK AGAIN; IT ISN'T WHAT IT SEEMS.`

segments.voice: Picture a fear that has gripped you lately, a scene your mind showed you of something terrible happening. Breathe slowly, and with each breath ask, in Vibhishana's calm voice, what you actually know, until the picture loosens its hold a little.
Indrajit's death. It begins with his cruelest trick, a magic Sita cut down before the army, and Vibhishana seeing through it to the fire at Nikumbhila.
Your line: it isn't what it seems. The race reaches the grove next. Day six hundred fifty-two.

653.title: Indrajit's death
653.hook: an uncle and a nephew face each other at the fire, and Lakshmana makes a vow on his brother's name
653.howItsDone: Lakshmana's vow before the final arrow, resting on Rama's righteousness and truth, is often quoted by Ramayana teachers as a picture of Lakshmana's devotion to his brother.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Indrajit's cruelest trick, a magic Sita cut down to stop the army, and Vibhishana saying look again. It isn't what it seems.

The grove at Nikumbhila is dark with trees, and somewhere inside, a fire is burning. Lakshmana's army crashes into the rakshasas guarding it, and the fighting gets so loud and close that Indrajit has to leave his offering unfinished and come out. He climbs into his chariot. And the first face he sees in the enemy line isn't Lakshmana's. It's his uncle's: Vibhishana, who knew about the fire, the grove and the secret condition, and brought them here.
screen: `THE FIRE IN THE GROVE.` → `THE RITE LEFT UNFINISHED.` → `HIS UNCLE'S FACE.`

segments.voice: Indrajit's words are bitter. You were born here, he says, you're my father's brother, and you've brought the enemy to your own nephew. You've thrown away your family and your people to serve strangers. Vibhishana answers without shouting. I was born among the rakshasas, he says, but my nature isn't cruel. I left my brother because of what he was doing: carrying off another man's wife, harming those who had done him no wrong. I couldn't take part in it. Both of them speak from loyalty; they just mean different things by it. Then the duel begins, Lakshmana and Indrajit, long and close: chariots wrecked, armor split, both men bleeding, neither giving way. At last Lakshmana fits to his bow the weapon of Indra, king of the gods, and before he lets it go, he speaks a vow. If Rama, son of Dasharatha, is righteous, true to his word and unmatched in courage, then let this arrow kill Ravana's son. The arrow flies, and Indrajit falls. Lakshmana doesn't rest the arrow on his own strength. He rests it on his brother's goodness. And the warrior named conqueror of Indra is brought down, at last, by Indra's own weapon. In Lanka, Ravana hears and loses his mind with grief. He grabs his sword and rushes toward the ashoka grove to kill Sita. A minister named Suparshva steps in front of him. You, a learned king, would kill a woman? Fight Rama instead. Ravana turns back.
screen: `YOU BETRAYED YOUR FAMILY.` · `MY NATURE ISN'T CRUEL.` · `A VOW ON RAMA'S GOODNESS.` · `SUPARSHVA STOPS THE SWORD.` · then, large: `BROUGHT DOWN BY INDRA'S OWN WEAPON.`

segments.voice: Let one person whose goodness you trust completely come to mind: a parent, a teacher, a friend. For a few slow breaths, let whatever you're facing rest on their steadiness, the way Lakshmana rested his arrow on Rama's goodness.

Your line: a vow on Rama's goodness. With his son gone, Ravana has no one left to send. Until tomorrow.

654.title: Ravana's final battle
654.hook: a spear meant for Vibhishana, a brother who steps in front of it, and a chariot sent from heaven
654.howItsDone: Ramlila performances across North India build toward Ravana's final battle over many nights. Many follow Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, where the wounding of Lakshmana that audiences know best comes earlier, from Meghnad (Indrajit), and Sushena and Hanuman's mountain save him there.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Indrajit's death at Nikumbhila, by Indra's own weapon, on a vow resting on Rama's goodness. A vow on Rama's goodness.

Ravana has no one left to send. His brother Kumbhakarna is dead. His son Indrajit is dead. Most of his champions are gone. So he puts on his armor, mounts his great chariot, and rides out through the gates himself, with whatever army remains. The monkeys scatter before him. And in the enemy line he sees the brother who left him, Vibhishana. Ravana picks up a great spear, made to kill, and aims it at him.
screen: `NO ONE LEFT TO SEND.` → `RAVANA RIDES OUT.` → `A SPEAR AIMED AT VIBHISHANA.`

segments.voice: Lakshmana sees it, and doesn't hesitate. He fires at Ravana again and again, drawing his attention away from Vibhishana. Remember Rama's vow on the beach: anyone who comes for refuge is safe. Lakshmana is keeping it with his own body. Ravana turns the spear on him. You saved him, he says, so take this instead. The spear strikes Lakshmana in the chest, and he falls. Rama pulls it out and breaks it, and then, Valmiki says, sits by his brother and weeps. What would I do with victory, with Sita even, without Lakshmana? This is where Valmiki's second herb flight comes. Sushena, the monkey physician, kneels and looks at Lakshmana's face. He isn't dead, he says; his face hasn't changed. He sends Hanuman to a mountain for herbs, and once more Hanuman comes back carrying a whole peak. Sushena crushes a herb and holds it to Lakshmana's nose, and he breathes it in and gets up. Then something else arrives from the sky. Rama has fought this whole war on foot, against a king in a chariot. The gods see it, and Indra sends his own chariot down to Rama, with his charioteer, Matali, holding the reins. Matali bows. This chariot is yours, he says. Rama walks around it with respect, and climbs aboard. For the first time, the two of them meet as equals: Ravana in his chariot, Rama in Indra's. The last battle can begin.
screen: `LAKSHMANA KEEPS RAMA'S VOW.` · `THE SPEAR STRIKES LAKSHMANA.` · `SUSHENA AND THE SECOND HERB.` · `INDRA'S CHARIOT AND MATALI.` · then, large: `FOR THE FIRST TIME, AS EQUALS.`

655.title: Ravana's final battle
655.hook: a sage with a hymn to the sun, heads that grow back, and one last arrow
655.carry: a hymn to the sun, and one arrow
655.howItsDone: Devotees recite the Aditya Hridayam, especially at sunrise, and on Dussehra (Vijayadashami) Ramlila performances in North India end with Ravana's effigy being burned.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana took a spear meant for Vibhishana, Sushena's herb brought him back, and Matali brought Indra's chariot down for Rama. Your line: as equals, at last.

The duel has gone on so long that Rama is worn out. He stands in Indra's chariot, tired to the bone, with Ravana in front of him ready to fight again. And in that pause, Valmiki says, the sage Agastya, who had come with the gods to watch, walks up to Rama on the battlefield: the same sage who gave Rama weapons years ago in the forest. This time he doesn't bring a weapon. He brings a hymn.
screen: `WORN OUT.` → `AGASTYA WALKS UP.` → `NOT A WEAPON. A HYMN.`

segments.voice: It's called the Aditya Hridayam, the heart of the sun, a hymn praising the sun as the source of light and life. Agastya teaches it to Rama there and then, and tells him to recite it three times. Rama does, facing the sun, and Valmiki says his weariness lifts and his heart fills with courage. The hymn is still recited today, often at sunrise, and some reach for it in exhausting stretches of their own lives. Then the fight resumes, and it's terrifying. Rama cuts off one of Ravana's heads with an arrow, and another grows in its place. Again and again, Valmiki says, a hundred times. Ravana can't be ended this way. Matali, the charioteer, leans over and reminds Rama of something he's carried all along: the weapon of Brahma, given to him long ago by Agastya. Rama takes it up. It blazes, Valmiki says, like the fire at the end of time. He charges it with the proper mantra, draws his bow to the full, and lets it go. The arrow strikes Ravana in the chest, and he falls from his chariot. Then, the text says, it returns to Rama's quiver. The gods rain flowers. The monkeys roar. Vibhishana stands over his fallen brother. On Dussehra, also called Vijayadashami, towns in North India set giant effigies of Ravana alight to mark this victory. In the book, the moment is quieter: a tired man, a hymn to the sun, and one arrow.
screen: `THE HEART OF THE SUN.` · `HEADS THAT GROW BACK.` · `MATALI: THE BRAHMA WEAPON.` · `RAVANA FALLS.` · then, large: `A TIRED MAN, A HYMN, ONE ARROW.`

segments.voice: If you can, turn toward a window or wherever the sun is, and admit any tiredness honestly, the way Rama faced his. Breathe in as if breathing in that light and breathe out the weariness; if you pray, offer a few words of thanks to the sun in your own way, and if not, simply resting in the light is enough.
Aditya Hridayam. The hymn to the sun that Agastya teaches Rama, lifting his weariness before the weapon of Brahma, at last, ends the war.
Your line: a hymn to the sun, and one arrow. When the noise dies down, someone comes out of the city to grieve. Day six hundred fifty-five, done.

656.title: Mandodari
656.hook: Ravana's queen walks onto the battlefield, and says what no one else could say
656.howItsDone: Some Hindus recite a traditional verse naming five revered women of the epics, the pañcakanyā, with Mandodari among them, and some say it in the morning; versions differ on one of the names.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Aditya Hridayam. A hymn to the sun lifted Rama's weariness, and one arrow ended the war.

When the noise of victory dies down, the gates of Lanka open, and the women of Ravana's palace come out onto the battlefield. They've lost husbands, sons, brothers. They walk among the dead, weeping, until they find him. One of them comes forward and kneels by the body. She is Mandodari, Ravana's chief queen, Indrajit's mother. She has lost her son, and now her husband. Valmiki lets her speak over him at length.
screen: `THE GATES OPEN.` → `THE WOMEN COME OUT.` → `MANDODARI KNEELS.`

segments.voice: Her lament holds love and truth at the same time. She remembers who he was. You frightened the gods, she says. Indra himself feared you. The earth and the mountains trembled at your name. How could a man on foot, wandering in the forest, bring you down? Then she answers her own question, in two ways. First, she says Rama can't be only a man. In Valmiki's words, as she grieves, he must be the eternal, the supreme, Vishnu himself, come in human form. A queen of Lanka is the one who says it out loud, over her husband's body. Then she turns to Ravana's own part in it, gently and without flinching. Long ago, she says, you conquered your senses, and with that discipline you conquered the three worlds. Now it's as if your senses remembered, and took their revenge. Your desire for Sita did what no army could. She says she warned him. She says Sita's faithfulness was a fire he couldn't hold. And then she simply grieves: her husband, her son, her life in pieces. She falls across his chest and weeps. Later tradition honored her. A well-known Sanskrit verse names five women of the epics whose remembrance is said to wash away wrongdoing, and Mandodari is one of them. Valmiki's portrait suggests why. She's loyal without being blind. She sees her husband whole, the greatness and the ruin, and she mourns him anyway.
screen: `YOU FRIGHTENED THE GODS.` · `RAMA IS MORE THAN A MAN.` · `YOUR SENSES TOOK REVENGE.` · `ONE OF THE FIVE WOMEN.` · then, large: `LOYAL WITHOUT BEING BLIND.`

segments.voice: Let someone you love who has real faults come to mind, perhaps someone you've lost, and see them whole, as Mandodari did. Breathe in with the love and out with the honesty, and let the two sit together without arguing.

657.title: Mandodari
657.hook: after Mandodari's grief, a funeral, a coronation, and two acts of mercy
657.howItsDone: Rama's words that enmity ends at death (maraṇāntāni vairāṇi) and Sita's mercy toward her guards are quoted by Hindu teachers on forgiveness and on treating the dead with respect.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mandodari, kneeling by Ravana, naming his greatness and his fault in one breath. Loyal without being blind.

Mandodari's lament ends. The other women lift her gently and lead her back toward the city. Ravana's body still lies on the field. Someone has to perform his funeral rites, and by custom that duty falls to his closest kin: Vibhishana. But Vibhishana stands back. He tells Rama he can't do it. This man was cruel, he says, he wronged others' wives, he was against everything right. How can I honor him?

segments.voice: Rama's answer is short, and it is still quoted. Enmity ends at death. Our purpose is finished. Perform his rites. He is mine now, as much as he is yours. Think about who's saying this: the man whose wife Ravana stole, whose brother Ravana nearly killed. The moment the war is over, Rama refuses to carry the hatred one step further. Ravana was a great warrior, he says, and deserves a king's funeral. So Vibhishana does it, with fire and ritual, as a brother. Mandodari saw Ravana whole; Rama lets him be honored whole. Then Rama has Vibhishana crowned king of Lanka, properly this time, and sends Hanuman into the city with the news for Sita. There a second mercy waits. Hanuman finds Sita in the grove, surrounded by the rakshasi guards who threatened her for months. He tells her Ravana is dead, and she's too moved to speak. Then he offers, angrily, to kill every one of the guards. Sita stops him. They were servants following a king's orders, she says. And then, in Valmiki, she says something that sounds like a whole teaching. A noble person shows compassion to the guilty and the good alike, because no one is without fault. Two people with every reason for revenge, Rama and Sita, on the same day, both refuse it.

658.howItsDone: Hindu teachers, scholars and storytellers discuss this scene from many sides, and some retellings, including women's songs and regional Ramayanas, give Sita's side of it at length.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama's words, enmity ends at death, Ravana's funeral rites, and Sita sparing the guards who tormented her.

For months, everything in this story has pointed to one moment. The search parties, the leap, the ring, the jewel, the bridge, the war. Now Vibhishana brings Sita out of the grove, bathed and dressed in fine clothes, carried toward Rama through a crowd of monkeys and rakshasas pressing to see her. Rama says: let her walk, so everyone can see. She steps down and walks toward him, shy and full of joy, looking at his face. What happens next has troubled readers, inside the tradition and out.
screen: `EVERYTHING POINTED HERE.` → `SITA WALKS TOWARD HIM.` → `WHAT HAPPENS NEXT.`

segments.voice: Rama does not take her in his arms. In Valmiki he speaks coldly, in front of everyone. I've won you back, he says, and wiped out the insult to my family's name. But know this: I didn't fight this war for you. I fought it for my honor and my family's. Then come the words that hurt most. She lived in another man's house for a long time, and he doesn't feel he can take her back. She's free to go wherever she likes, he says, and he even names men she could go to. Valmiki doesn't soften it. Sita weeps, ashamed in front of the crowd, shrinking as if into herself, and those watching are shaken too. People within the tradition have argued about this passage for a long time. Some teachers say Rama speaks as a king, not a husband: a king must be seen to be beyond suspicion, and he's performing for his people, not speaking from his heart. Some read it as a test meant for the world rather than for Sita. Other readers, Hindu and not, find it simply wrong, say so, and side with Sita. The epic has room for all those readers. Tomorrow, Sita answers. So a week that began with an illusion of her death, then a vow at Nikumbhila, a hymn to the sun, a queen's lament and a funeral, closes on her standing before the man she waited for, hearing words she never expected.

Breathe in and rest a kind hand there in your imagination, then breathe out and let it be held, because being hurt by words is real.
